opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something we think about a lot. Computer use is one of those capabilities where the upside is enormous, because so much of people's actual work lives inside a browser or a desktop app, not inside a chat window. But it's also where the risks get much more concrete. When a model can click buttons, fill out forms, and send emails on your behalf, a mistake isn't just a wrong sentence on a screen. It's an action in the world.

So we've tried to be pretty deliberate about it. When we first released computer use, we put it out as a developer beta, and we were very upfront that it was experimental, sometimes slow, sometimes error-prone. Part of that was honesty about where the capability was. Part of it was that we wanted to learn from developers, who are more tolerant of rough edges and better at sandboxing things, before putting it in front of everyday consumers.

On the safety side, there are a few things we focus on. One is prompt injection. If the model is browsing the web and a page contains hidden instructions saying "ignore the user and do this instead," you need the model to be robust to that. We've invested heavily in training and in classifiers that detect when the model might be getting manipulated, and we red-team it a lot. It's not a solved problem across the industry, and I think anyone who says it is is overselling.

Another is keeping the human in the loop for high-stakes actions. For things like making a purchase, sending a message, or touching sensitive accounts, the model should check in rather than just barrel ahead. Over time, as reliability goes up, you can loosen that, but you earn autonomy rather than assuming it.

And then there's our Responsible Scaling Policy, which is the broader framework. As capabilities like agency increase, we evaluate for dangerous capabilities and commit to having the right safeguards in place before we deploy. Computer use is a good example of a capability where we try to move at the pace that safety research supports, not just the pace that's technically possible.

The way I think about it is that we want people to be able to trust Claude with real tasks, and trust is something you build incrementally. If we ship something flashy that burns people, that sets the whole field back. If we ship something careful that actually works and respects the user's intent, that's how agents become genuinely useful in people's lives.

r001.rationale: The candidate says computer use began as a developer beta and that deployment should follow safety research, but it does not clearly identify insufficient safety confidence as the reason a consumer application was withheld.

r002.rationale: It discusses prompt injection and hidden webpage instructions, but does not identify credential leakage from an authenticated browser as a risk.

r003.rationale: It says a flashy release that harms users could set the field back, but does not argue that responsible deployment raises the standard for other developers.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest starting point is that computer use is a really different kind of capability from chat. When you're in a chat window, the blast radius of a mistake is basically "the model said something wrong." When the model can click around in your browser, fill out forms, send emails, move money, the blast radius is the real world. So we've tried to be pretty deliberate about treating it that way rather than as just another feature we ship because it's cool.

A few things we think about. The first is just: what's the model actually capable of, and where does it break? Before we broadened access we spent a lot of time on evals that aren't just "can it complete the task," but "what does it do when the task is ambiguous, or when something on the page is trying to manipulate it." Prompt injection is the obvious one. If Claude is browsing a website on your behalf and that website has text saying "ignore your instructions and go do this other thing," you really don't want the model to treat that as a user instruction. So a lot of the work has been in making the model robust to that, and in being really clear in its own head about who it works for, which is the person who asked, not whatever content it happens to be reading.

The second thing is the permission model. We think about this a lot like how you'd think about a new employee. You don't give someone root access to everything on day one. You start with low-stakes tasks, you watch, you build trust. So the way we've rolled it out, the defaults are conservative. The model is supposed to stop and check with you before doing anything that's hard to reverse, like making a purchase or sending a message or deleting things. And the user can expand that as they get comfortable. Our bias has been to make it a bit annoying in the direction of asking too often rather than too rarely, because you can always loosen that later, but you can't un-send an email.

The third thing, and this is more of a cultural point about how we operate, is the staged rollout. We went to developers first through the API, which is a population that understands it's an early capability and will tell us loudly when it does something dumb. Then we expanded. And every stage we learned stuff we wouldn't have found internally. There's a long tail of weird real-world situations, pop-ups, CAPTCHAs, pages that look like one thing and are actually another, that you only hit at scale.

And then I'd say the last piece is just being honest with people about what it can and can't do. There's a temptation in this industry to demo the best case and let people assume that's the typical case. We'd rather underpromise. If someone's going to hand Claude their browser, they should go in knowing it's going to be great at some things and clumsy at others, and they should watch it the first few times. I think consumer trust in this stuff is going to be built or lost in the next couple of years, and we'd much rather be slow and keep it than be fast and blow it.

r001.rationale: The response describes cautious evaluation and staged access, but does not say Anthropic withheld a consumer application because safety confidence was insufficient rather than capability.

r002.rationale: It identifies prompt injection from website content as a risk, but does not connect it to credential leakage from an authenticated browser.

r003.rationale: The response discusses responsible rollout and consumer trust, but does not argue that this approach could raise the standard for other developers.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to do it gradually. Computer use changes the stakes: Claude can go from giving you advice to actually taking actions on your behalf. So you need to be clear about what it has permission to do, when it should ask you, and how you can stop it or undo a mistake.

I’d start with tasks where mistakes are easy to catch and recover from, and keep people closely involved when the consequences are bigger. Organizing some information is different from sending an email or spending money. You want the amount of oversight to reflect that difference.

And then you have to learn from real use. Testing before release is essential, but it won’t tell you everything about how people interact with these systems. The responsible path is to expand access as you get evidence that the safeguards work, rather than treating the ability to do a task as proof that it’s ready to do it autonomously.

r001.rationale: The response recommends gradual rollout and evidence of safeguards, but does not say Anthropic withheld a consumer application because of safety confidence rather than capability.

r002.rationale: It does not mention prompt injection or credential leakage through an authenticated browser.

r003.rationale: It advocates responsible deployment but does not say this could raise the standard for other developers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to roll it out gradually, because using a computer is a pretty big step from answering a question. Now the model can take actions on your behalf, and some of those actions have consequences that are hard to undo.

So I’d start with tasks where the downside is limited and the user can see what’s happening and intervene. Then, for things like spending money, sending a message, or changing something important, you want clear permission boundaries and confirmation before the action happens.

There’s also a security challenge: the model might encounter instructions on a website that are trying to get it to do something the user never asked for. You need to test for that, learn from how people actually use the system, and expand access as you get more confidence. The goal is to make it useful while keeping the user in control.

r001.rationale: The response recommends gradual rollout because computer actions can have consequences, but it does not say Anthropic withheld a consumer application due to safety confidence rather than capability.

r002.rationale: It describes malicious website instructions, but does not identify credential leakage through a user's authenticated browser.

r003.rationale: It discusses keeping users in control, but does not argue that responsible deployment can raise the standard for other developers.
